questions.q: Find the equation of the line perpendicular to $y=\dfrac{1}{2}x+3$ passing through $(4,1)$.
questions.answer: The perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal: $m=-2$. $y-1=-2(x-4)$, so $y=-2x+8+1=-2x+9$.

sections.heading: Finding equations from two points or a table

questions.q: A linear function passes through $(0,5)$ and $(4,17)$. Find its equation.
questions.answer: Slope $=\dfrac{17-5}{4-0}=\dfrac{12}{4}=3$. Since $(0,5)$ is the $y$-intercept, the equation is $y=3x+5$.

Solve the inequality $3x-4<11$, and graph the solution on a number line description.
questions.answer: $3x<15$, so $x<5$. On a number line, this is an open circle at $5$ with shading extending to the left (all values less than 5).

questions.q: Solve the inequality $-2x+7\geq1$, being careful with the direction of the inequality sign.
A system requires $y>2x-1$ and $y\leq-x+5$. Determine whether the point $(1,2)$ satisfies both inequalities.
questions.answer: Check the first: $2>2(1)-1=1$? True. Check the second: $2\leq-1+5=4$? True. Since $(1,2)$ satisfies both inequalities, it lies in the solution region.

questions.q: A student has $50$ dollars and wants to buy notebooks costing $6$ dollars each, keeping at least $8$ dollars in reserve. Write an inequality for the number of notebooks $n$ the student can buy, and solve it.
questions.answer: The amount spent, $6n$, must leave at least 8 dollars: $50-6n\geq8$, so $-6n\geq-42$, giving $n\leq7$ (dividing by a negative number flips the inequality). The student can buy at most 7 notebooks.

questions.q: A factory produces at least 200 units per day but at most 350 units per day. Write a compound inequality for the daily production $p$, and state whether $p=180$ is a valid production level.
questions.answer: $200\leq p\leq350$. Since $180<200$, the value $p=180$ does NOT satisfy the inequality — it is below the minimum required production level.

sections.heading: Comparing rates of change between two linear functions

questions.q: Function $f$ is given by $f(x)=3x+2$. Function $g$ is defined by the table: $x=0,g=1$ and $x=2,g=9$. Which function has the greater rate of change?
questions.answer: $f$ has a rate of change (slope) of $3$. For $g$: slope $=\dfrac{9-1}{2-0}=\dfrac{8}{2}=4$. Since $4>3$, function $g$ has the greater rate of change.

sections.heading: Finding the intersection of two lines graphically and algebraically

questions.q: Two lines are given by $y=2x-1$ and $y=-x+8$. Find their point of intersection, and explain what this point represents graphically.
questions.answer: Set equal: $2x-1=-x+8$, so $3x=9$, giving $x=3$. Then $y=2(3)-1=5$. The lines intersect at $(3,5)$, which represents the single point where both lines cross on a graph — the unique solution to the system formed by the two equations.

sections.heading: Writing a linear inequality from a verbal description

questions.q: A shipping company charges 3 dollars per pound but offers free shipping if the package weighs less than 2 pounds. Write a piecewise description of the cost $C(w)$ as a function of weight $w$, and find the cost of a 5-pound package.
questions.answer: $C(w)=0$ for $w<2$ and $C(w)=3w$ for $w\geq2$. For a 5-pound package: $C(5)=3(5)=15$ dollars.

questions.q: A parking garage charges 5 dollars for the first hour and 2 dollars for each additional hour. Write an equation for the total cost $C$ after $h$ hours (for $h\geq1$), and find the cost for 6 hours.
questions.answer: $C(h)=5+2(h-1)$ for $h\geq1$ (since only the hours after the first are charged at the additional rate). For 6 hours: $C(6)=5+2(5)=5+10=15$ dollars.

sections.heading: Graphing a system of inequalities and identifying the feasible region

questions.q: A system requires $x+y\leq10$ and $x\geq2$ and $y\geq0$. Determine which of the points $(3,4)$ and $(8,5)$ lie in the feasible (solution) region, checking each condition.
questions.answer: For $(3,4)$: $3+4=7\leq10$ ✓, $3\geq2$ ✓, $4\geq0$ ✓ — all conditions satisfied, so $(3,4)$ is in the feasible region. For $(8,5)$: $8+5=13\leq10$? False — this point fails the first condition, so $(8,5)$ is NOT in the feasible region.

sections.heading: Rate of change from a real-world linear model

questions.q: A water tank starts with 500 gallons and drains at a constant rate. After 4 hours, it contains 340 gallons. Write a linear equation for the volume $V$ after $t$ hours, and predict when the tank will be empty.
questions.answer: Rate of change: $\dfrac{340-500}{4-0}=\dfrac{-160}{4}=-40$ gallons per hour. Equation: $V=500-40t$. The tank is empty when $V=0$: $500-40t=0$, so $t=12.5$ hours.

questions.q: Find the equation of the line perpendicular to $y=-\frac{2}{3}x-6$ passing through $(5,3)$, in slope-intercept form.
questions.answer: The perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal, $m=\frac{3}{2}$. $y-(3)=\frac{3}{2}(x-(5))$, so $y=\frac{3}{2}x-\frac{9}{2}$.

questions.q: Find the equation of the line perpendicular to $y=x+3$ passing through $(-4,-8)$, in slope-intercept form.
questions.answer: The perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal, $m=-1$. $y-(-8)=-1(x-(-4))$, so $y=-x-12$.

questions.q: Find the equation of the line parallel to $y=-3x+1$ passing through $(4,-3)$, in slope-intercept form.
questions.answer: Parallel lines share the same slope, $m=-3$. $y-(-3)=-3(x-(4))$, so $y=-3x+9$.

questions.q: Find the equation of the line parallel to $y=\frac{1}{2}x-5$ passing through $(4,-3)$, in slope-intercept form.
questions.answer: Parallel lines share the same slope, $m=\frac{1}{2}$. $y-(-3)=\frac{1}{2}(x-(4))$, so $y=\frac{1}{2}x-5$.

questions.q: Find the equation of the line parallel to $y=\frac{1}{3}x-7$ passing through $(2,8)$, in slope-intercept form.
questions.answer: Parallel lines share the same slope, $m=\frac{1}{3}$. $y-(8)=\frac{1}{3}(x-(2))$, so $y=\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{22}{3}$.

A student has $127$ dollars and wants to buy raffle entries costing $13$ dollars each, keeping at least $10$ dollars in reserve. Find the maximum number of raffle entries the student can buy.
questions.answer: $127-13n\geq10$, so $-13n\geq-117$, giving $n\leq9$ (dividing by a negative number flips the inequality). The student can buy at most 9 raffle entries.
